lessons.title: What a container is
lessons.intro: This course is about Docker: packaging a program with everything it needs, and running that package the same way on any machine. It is a reading course. Each module explains a few ideas, shows them as commands, files and diagrams, asks you to judge some situations, and ends with a short exercise and one possible answer. Nothing in the course is run for you. If Docker is installed you can type the commands yourself, and the course works without it. The examples use one running product: a small web service called tracker, and the database it stores its data in.

steps.title: The problem
steps.text:
A program rarely runs alone. It needs a runtime of the right version, libraries, system tools, files in certain places, and settings. On the machine where it was written, all of that is already there. On the next machine, some of it is missing or a different version, and the program fails in a way nobody can reproduce.

The usual fix is a page of setup instructions. Instructions go out of date, and two people following them still end up with different machines.

Docker takes another approach. You package the program **together with** its runtime, libraries and files, and you run that package as a unit. The machine only needs Docker.

steps.title: Images and containers
steps.text:
Two words carry the whole course.

- An **image** is the package. It is a read-only set of files (the program, its runtime, its libraries) plus a note saying which command to start. An image does nothing by itself. It sits on disk.
- A **container** is a running instance of an image. Docker starts the command from the image, and gives it a private copy of the image's files to work in.

One image can be started many times. Each start gives a separate container with its own files, its own processes and its own network address. Changes made inside one container are not seen by the others, and they do not change the image.

steps.title: One image, two containers
steps.text: Two containers, A and B, are started from the same image. A program in container A writes a file to `/tmp/report.txt`.

steps.title: What a container isolates
steps.text:
A container is not a small computer. It is one or more ordinary processes running on the host machine, started with a restricted view of it. The process inside sees:

- **Its own files.** The root folder `/` is the image's files, not the host's.
- **Its own processes.** It cannot see or signal the host's other processes.
- **Its own network.** It has its own address and its own ports.
- **Its own limits.** The host can cap how much memory and processor time it uses.

On Linux these come from two features of the operating system core (the kernel). **Namespaces** control what a process can see. **Control groups** (cgroups) control how much it may use. Docker is the tool that sets them up for you.

One thing is not private: the kernel itself. Every container on a host uses the host's kernel.

steps.title: Containers and virtual machines
steps.text:
A virtual machine also isolates software, and the two are often confused. The difference is where the boundary sits.

A virtual machine pretends to be hardware. It runs a complete operating system with its own kernel. That takes gigabytes of disk and tens of seconds to start.

A container shares the host's kernel and holds only the program and its files. It is usually tens or hundreds of megabytes and starts in about the time the program itself takes to start.

Sharing the kernel has two consequences worth remembering. The boundary is thinner than a virtual machine's, which matters for security and is the subject of a later module. And a Linux container needs a Linux kernel. On macOS and Windows, Docker Desktop quietly runs a small Linux virtual machine and puts your containers inside it.

steps.title: Which kernel?
steps.text: An image was built from Ubuntu files. It is run on a server that uses a different Linux distribution.

steps.title: The parts of Docker
steps.text:
Three parts work together.

- The **client** is the `docker` command you type.
- The **daemon** (also called the engine) is a background service that does the work: it builds images, starts containers and manages their storage and networks. The client only sends it requests.
- A **registry** is a server that stores images so that other machines can download them. Docker Hub is the public one that Docker uses when you name no other.

Most commands in this course follow one path: you type a command, the client sends it to the daemon, and the daemon fetches an image from a registry if it does not have it yet.

steps.title: Exercise: image or container?
steps.text:
Take a few minutes. For each statement, decide whether it describes an image, a container, or neither.

1. It can be copied to a registry and downloaded by another machine.
2. It has a process list.
3. It includes its own kernel.
4. It is read-only.
5. It can be stopped and started again.
6. Deleting it loses the files a program wrote while running.

Then continue to compare.

steps.title: One possible answer
steps.text:
1. **Image.** Registries store images. A container is not shipped anywhere.
2. **Container.** Only something running has processes.
3. **Neither.** A container uses the host's kernel, and an image holds only files. A virtual machine is what includes a kernel.
4. **Image.** A container adds a private writable area on top of it.
5. **Container.** An image is never running, so there is nothing to stop.
6. **Container.** Files written inside a container live in that container's writable area and are removed with it. A later module shows where to keep data that must survive.

If you remember one sentence from this module, make it this one: an image is a package of files, and a container is a process started from it.

questions.prompt: Can a program in container B read that file?

choices.text: Yes, both share the image's files
choices.feedback: They share the read-only image. Anything a container writes goes to its own private area.

choices.text: No, each container has its own files
choices.feedback: Each container gets a private writable area on top of the image. B never sees what A wrote, and the image is unchanged.

choices.text: Yes, after A stops
choices.feedback: Stopping A does not move its files anywhere. They stay in A's private area until A is removed.

questions.prompt: Which kernel do the processes in the container use?

choices.text: The server's kernel
choices.feedback: A container has no kernel of its own. The image supplies files such as tools and libraries, and the host supplies the kernel.

choices.text: Ubuntu's kernel, from the image
choices.feedback: An image holds files for programs to use. It does not hold a running kernel, and a container cannot boot one.

choices.text: A small kernel that Docker adds
choices.feedback: Docker adds no kernel. On macOS and Windows it runs a Linux virtual machine, and containers share that machine's kernel.

lessons.title: Run and manage containers
lessons.intro: This module covers the commands used every day: starting a container, seeing what is running, reading its output, getting inside it, and cleaning up. The main idea is the life of a container. It exists from the moment it is created until it is removed, and it is running only while its main process is alive.

steps.title: What docker run does
steps.text:
`docker run` takes an image name and starts a container from it.

```bash
docker run nginx:1.27
```

Four things happen, in order.

1. Docker looks for the image `nginx:1.27` on this machine.
2. If it is missing, Docker downloads it from the registry. This is called a **pull**.
3. Docker creates a container: a private writable area on top of the image, a network address, and a name.
4. Docker starts the image's main command inside it.

Run like this, the container holds on to your terminal and prints the program's output. Pressing Ctrl+C stops it.

steps.title: In the background, with a name
steps.text:
A service should not hold a terminal. Two options fix that.

- `-d` (detached) starts the container in the background and prints its identifier.
- `--name` gives it a name you choose. Without one Docker invents a name such as `brave_wilson`.

`docker ps` lists the running containers. Every later command accepts either the name or the first few characters of the identifier.

steps.title: The life of a container
steps.text:
A container is **running** while its main process is alive. When that process ends, for any reason, the container stops. Docker does not keep an empty container running.

A stopped container still exists. Its files and its output are kept, and it can be started again. It is gone only when you remove it.

`docker ps` shows only running containers. `docker ps -a` shows stopped ones too, with the code the main process ended with.

steps.title: A command that finishes
steps.text:
You run this, and it prints `hello`.

```bash
docker run ubuntu:24.04 echo hello
```

steps.title: Stop, start and remove
steps.text:
| Command | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `docker stop web` | Asks the main process to end, waits up to 10 seconds, then forces it. |
| `docker start web` | Starts a stopped container again, with the files it had. |
| `docker restart web` | Stop, then start. |
| `docker rm web` | Removes a stopped container and its private files. |
| `docker rm -f web` | Forces a running container to end, then removes it. |

Removing is the step people forget. Every `docker run` creates a new container, so a machine collects stopped ones over time.

For a container you will not need again, add `--rm` to `docker run`. Docker then removes the container as soon as it stops.

steps.title: Look at a running container
steps.text:
Two commands answer most questions about a container.

`docker logs` prints what the main process wrote to its output. Add `-f` to keep following it, and `--tail 50` to see only the last lines. Logs are kept after the container stops, until it is removed.

`docker exec` runs an extra command inside a container that is already running. With `-it` it gives you an interactive terminal, which is how you open a shell inside one.

Keep `run` and `exec` apart. `run` creates a **new** container. `exec` goes into an **existing** one.

steps.title: A crowded list
steps.text: This is `docker ps -a` on a developer's machine after a week of work.

steps.title: Containers you type into
steps.text:
A container does not have to be a service. It can be a throwaway place to try a tool without installing it.

```bash
docker run --rm -it ubuntu:24.04 bash
```

`-i` keeps the input open and `-t` gives the program a terminal, so together they give you a working shell. The shell is the container's main process. When you type `exit`, the main process ends, the container stops, and `--rm` removes it. Nothing is left on your machine except the image.

steps.title: Exercise: a day with one container
steps.text:
Write the command for each step. Use the image `nginx:1.27` and the name `web`.

1. Start it in the background.
2. Check that it is running.
3. See the last 20 lines of its output.
4. Open a shell inside it.
5. Stop it and remove it.
6. Run `nginx -v` in a fresh container of the same image, leaving nothing behind.

steps.title: One possible answer
steps.text:
The commands are below. Two points are worth noticing.

Step 5 can be one command, `docker rm -f web`, when you do not care how the program shuts down. Stopping first gives it the chance to finish its work.

In step 6 the words after the image name replace the image's usual command. The container runs `nginx -v`, prints the version, and ends. `--rm` removes it.

questions.prompt: What state is the container in afterwards?

choices.text: Running, waiting for another command
choices.feedback: A container runs only while its main process is alive. `echo` ended, so the container stopped.

choices.text: Removed
choices.feedback: Nothing removes it unless you add `--rm` or run `docker rm`.

choices.text: Stopped, and still listed by `docker ps -a`
choices.feedback: The main process ended with code 0, so the container stopped. It stays on disk until it is removed.

questions.prompt: Which habit would have prevented most of this list?

choices.text: Adding `--rm` to one-off runs
choices.feedback: Each of those rows is a finished one-off command. With `--rm` every one would have been removed when it ended.

choices.text: Using `-d` on every run
choices.feedback: Running in the background does not remove anything. The stopped containers would still pile up.

choices.text: Pulling the image first
choices.feedback: Pulling affects the image, not the containers. Each `docker run` still creates a new container.

lessons.title: Name and find images
lessons.intro: Every container starts from an image, and every image has a name. This module covers how to read that name, why a tag is weaker than it looks, what a digest guarantees, and how to choose where your images come from.

steps.title: The parts of an image name
steps.text:
An image name has up to four parts.

- The **registry** is the server the image is stored on.
- The **repository** is the image's path on that server, often a team and a product.
- The **tag** names one version of it.
- The **digest**, when present, identifies the exact content.

Short names work because of defaults. With no registry, Docker uses Docker Hub. With no team on Docker Hub, it uses `library`, which holds the official images. With no tag, it uses `latest`. So `nginx` really means `docker.io/library/nginx:latest`.

steps.title: A tag can move
steps.text:
A tag is a label that the publisher attaches to an image, and the publisher can move it to another image at any time.

That is how updates arrive. `nginx:1.27` points at the newest 1.27 release, and it moves each time a fix is published. This is useful, and it also means the name does not identify one fixed set of files.

`latest` deserves special care. It is only the tag used when you name none. Nothing makes it the newest version, and it can jump to a new major version without warning.

steps.title: The same name, a month apart
steps.text: A build server pulls `node:24-slim` today. A second server pulls `node:24-slim` a month from now.

steps.title: A digest cannot
steps.text:
A **digest** is a fingerprint worked out from the image's content, written as `sha256:` and 64 characters. Change one byte of the image and the digest changes.

You can name an image by digest in place of a tag. That name can only ever mean those exact files. If a registry returned anything else, Docker would refuse it.

The cost is that a digest never picks up fixes. Somebody has to change it deliberately. Many teams accept that cost for what runs in production, because they want every change to be a decision.

steps.title: Choosing a tag
steps.text:
| You write | You get | Good for |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `node` or `node:latest` | Whatever is newest today | Quick experiments only |
| `node:24` | The newest release of version 24 | Development |
| `node:24.11.1` | One release, rebuilt when its base is patched | Builds you want to repeat |
| `node:24.11.1@sha256:...` | Exactly one image | Production |

Many images also come in variants, named in the tag after a hyphen. `-slim` leaves out tools most programs do not need. `-alpine` is built on a very small Linux distribution. The module on small images compares them.

A reasonable default is a specific version with a variant, such as `node:24.11.1-slim`, updated on purpose.

steps.title: Where images come from
steps.text:
Anyone can publish to a public registry. An image is software that you are about to run, so who published it matters as much as it does for any download.

- **Official images** are maintained and reviewed for Docker Hub. Their names have no team part: `nginx`, `postgres`, `node`.
- **Publisher images** come from the company that makes the software, under its own name.
- **Everything else** is a stranger's build. Read how it was made before you depend on it, or build your own.

Images are kept on your machine after the first pull. `docker pull` fetches one without running it, `docker image ls` lists what you have, and `docker image rm` deletes one.

steps.title: Two unpinned names
steps.text: These two lines come from the files that describe a team's production service.

steps.title: Images are made of layers
steps.text:
Watch a pull and you will see several lines, each with its own identifier. An image is a stack of **layers**, and each layer is a set of file changes.

Layers are shared. If two images are built on the same base, the base layers are downloaded and stored once. That is why the second pull of a related image is much faster than the first.

The next two modules show where layers come from and how to use them well.

steps.title: Exercise: read and choose
steps.text:
First, name the registry, repository and tag of each.

1. `postgres`
2. `ghcr.io/acme/tracker:1.4.2`
3. `registry.example.com:5000/tools/backup`

Then choose how to name the image in each situation, and say why.

4. Trying out a database on your laptop for an afternoon.
5. The base image in a project five people build every day.
6. The database a production service runs on.

steps.title: One possible answer
steps.text:
1. Registry `docker.io`, repository `library/postgres`, tag `latest`. All three are defaults.
2. Registry `ghcr.io`, repository `acme/tracker`, tag `1.4.2`.
3. Registry `registry.example.com:5000`, repository `tools/backup`, tag `latest`. The `:5000` is a port of the registry, not a tag, because a tag comes after the last slash.

4. `postgres:17` is enough. Nothing depends on it tomorrow.
5. A specific version and variant, such as `node:24.11.1-slim`. Everyone builds from the same release, and updating it is a change the team can see.
6. A specific version with its digest. An upgrade of a production database should be planned, never a side effect of a restart.

choices.feedback: A tag is a label the publisher can move. The same name can point at a newer image a month later.

choices.text: Not necessarily, the tag may have moved
choices.feedback: `24-slim` follows new releases of version 24. Only a digest names one fixed image.

choices.text: Yes, unless the major version changed
choices.feedback: The major version stays 24, but minor and patch releases still replace what the tag points at.

questions.prompt: What is the main risk?

choices.text: The images will be large
choices.feedback: Size depends on the variant. The concern here is that neither line says which version is meant.

choices.text: Docker Hub may refuse the pull
choices.feedback: Both names are valid. They resolve to `latest`.

choices.text: A restart or rebuild can bring in a different version
choices.feedback: Both resolve to `latest`. A new major version of the runtime or the database can arrive without anyone choosing it.

lessons.title: Write a Dockerfile
lessons.intro: So far every image came from someone else. This module covers building your own. A Dockerfile is a short text file that lists the steps to make an image. You will read one line by line, learn which files the build can see, and keep the wrong files out.

steps.title: A recipe for an image
steps.text:
A **Dockerfile** is a list of instructions, run from top to bottom. Each starts with a word in capitals. The result is an image.

The file below packages the tracker service. Read it as a set of setup notes that a machine follows exactly: start from an image that already has the runtime, make a folder, copy the list of dependencies, install them, copy the program, and note how to start it.

By convention the file is named `Dockerfile`, with no extension, and sits at the top of the project.

steps.title: The instructions you need
steps.text:
| Instruction | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `FROM` | Names the image to start from. Every Dockerfile begins with one. |
| `WORKDIR` | Sets the folder for the instructions that follow, and creates it. |
| `COPY` | Copies files from your project into the image. |
| `RUN` | Runs a command while building, and saves the result in the image. |
| `ENV` | Sets an environment variable in the image. |
| `EXPOSE` | Notes which port the program listens on. It opens nothing. |
| `USER` | Sets the user that later instructions and the container run as. |
| `CMD` | Records the command to start when a container runs. |

The pair to keep apart is `RUN` and `CMD`. `RUN` happens **once, during the build**, and its effect is stored in the image. `CMD` runs nothing during the build. It is a note that says what to start **each time a container runs**.

steps.title: Build time or run time?
steps.text: The Dockerfile contains `RUN npm ci`, which downloads the service's dependencies. The image is built once and then started on fifty servers.

steps.title: The build context
steps.text:
The build command ends with a path, usually a dot.

```bash
docker build -t tracker:dev .
```

That path is the **build context**: the folder whose files the build is allowed to use. `COPY` can read only from the context. It cannot reach `../other-project` or a file elsewhere on your disk.

The whole context is handed to the builder before the first instruction runs. A context with a few source files is sent in an instant. One that includes downloaded dependencies, build output and the version history can be hundreds of megabytes, and slow every build.

steps.title: Keep files out with .dockerignore
steps.text:
A file named `.dockerignore`, placed beside the Dockerfile, lists what to leave out of the context. Each line is a path or a pattern.

Leave out three kinds of file.

- **Things the build makes for itself**, such as installed dependencies and build output. Copies from your machine may be for the wrong system.
- **Things the image does not need**, such as the version history, editor settings and documentation.
- **Things that must never be in an image**, such as `.env` files, keys and certificates.

The last kind is the important one. A file that never enters the context cannot be copied into an image by accident.

steps.title: A broad copy
steps.text: A project folder holds the files listed below. Its Dockerfile has no `.dockerignore` beside it.

steps.title: Build it and run it
steps.text:
`docker build` reads the Dockerfile in the context and runs each instruction. `-t` gives the result a name and tag. Without it the image has only an identifier.

The image is stored on your machine like any other, and `docker run` starts it.

Build output is long. The lines worth reading are the numbered steps. When a step fails, the build stops there, prints that command's error, and makes no image.

steps.title: What belongs in an image
steps.text:
An image should hold what is the same everywhere the program runs: the program, its runtime and its dependencies.

Leave out what differs from place to place. Database addresses, feature switches and passwords are supplied when the container starts, which a later module covers. Data the program creates is kept outside the container, also covered later.

And keep to one concern per image. An image that starts a web server, a database and a scheduler together cannot be updated, scaled or restarted one part at a time. Three images, each doing one job, can.

steps.title: Exercise: a static site
steps.text:
A folder named `site` holds a small website: `index.html`, a stylesheet and some pictures. The official `nginx` image serves any files placed in `/usr/share/nginx/html`, and it already knows how to start itself.

1. Write a Dockerfile that produces an image serving this site.
2. Write the command that builds it as `site:1`.
3. The project folder also holds a `drafts` folder and a `.git` folder. Write a `.dockerignore`.

steps.text:

The tag on `FROM` is a specific version, following the last module. The `.dockerignore` is short, and it still matters: without it the drafts and the whole version history would be sent to the builder on every build, even though this Dockerfile copies only `site/`.

lessons.title: Use layers and the build cache
lessons.intro: A Dockerfile that works can still be slow to build and larger than it needs to be. Both problems have the same cause, which is how an image is stored: as a stack of layers. This module explains layers and the build cache, and shows how the order of instructions decides whether a rebuild takes a second or several minutes.

steps.title: Every step adds a layer
steps.text:
An image is a stack of **layers**. Each layer holds the files that one build step added, changed or removed, compared with the layers below it.

The instructions that change files each produce a layer: `FROM` brings in the base image's layers, and every `RUN` and `COPY` adds one more. Instructions such as `CMD`, `ENV` and `EXPOSE` change only the image's notes and add no files.

When a container starts, Docker stacks the layers and shows them as one folder tree. Layers are read-only and identified by their content, which is why two images built on the same base can share them.

steps.title: The cache rule
steps.text:
Building a layer can be slow, so the builder keeps every layer it makes. On the next build it reuses a kept layer when it can. This is the **build cache**.

The rule has two parts.

1. A step is reused if the instruction is the same as last time **and** its inputs are the same. For `COPY`, the inputs are the contents of the files being copied. For `RUN`, the input is the text of the command.
2. A step can be reused only if **every step above it** was reused. The first step that has to run again forces every later step to run again too.

So one change near the top of a Dockerfile rebuilds everything below it.

steps.title: One changed file
steps.text:
A Dockerfile contains these two lines in this order. You fix a typo in one source file and build again.

```dockerfile
COPY . .
RUN npm ci --omit=dev
```

steps.title: Order by how often things change
steps.text:
The fix is to put the things that change rarely near the top and the things that change often near the bottom.

In most projects the list of dependencies changes a few times a month, and the source code changes many times a day. So copy only the dependency list first, install, and copy the source last.

Now a change to a source file invalidates only the final `COPY`. The install step above it is reused, and the build takes a second or two.

steps.title: A deleted file is still in the image
steps.text:
Layers only add. If one step creates a file and a later step deletes it, the file is still stored in the earlier layer. The later layer merely hides it. The image is no smaller, and anyone with the image can read the hidden file by looking at that layer.

Two rules follow.

- **Clean up in the same `RUN` that made the mess.** Join the commands with `&&` so that the temporary files never reach a finished layer.
- **Never copy a secret in and delete it afterwards.** It remains in the image. The module on privilege shows the safe way to use a secret during a build.

steps.title: Two lines that should be one
steps.text: This fragment installs a system package. It was written three months ago and the first line has been cached ever since. Today someone adds a second package to the last line.

steps.title: See the layers
steps.text:
`docker history` lists an image's layers, newest first, with the instruction that made each one and its size. It is the quickest way to find out where an image's size comes from.

It is also a reminder that the instructions are not private. Anyone who has the image can read every line, including any value written into a `RUN` or `ENV`.

steps.title: Keep the download cache between builds
steps.text:
Even a well ordered file reinstalls everything when the dependency list does change. A **cache mount** softens that. It gives one `RUN` step a folder that is kept between builds and is not part of the image.

```dockerfile
RUN --mount=type=cache,target=/root/.npm npm ci --omit=dev
```

The package manager keeps its downloads in that folder. When the list changes, it fetches only what is new. The image gets the installed result and none of the download cache.

steps.title: Exercise: a slow build
steps.text:
This Dockerfile takes four minutes to rebuild after any change, even to a comment in a source file.

```dockerfile
FROM node:24.11.1-slim
WORKDIR /app
COPY . .
RUN apt-get update
RUN apt-get install -y curl
RUN npm ci --omit=dev
CMD ["node", "server.js"]
```

1. Say which steps run again after a one-line source change, and why.
2. Rewrite it so that such a change rebuilds as little as possible.
3. Fix anything else this module warned about.

steps.title: One possible answer
steps.text:
1. Everything from `COPY . .` down. The copied files changed, so that step runs, and every step after a step that ran must run as well: both `apt-get` lines and the install.

2. and 3. The rewrite is below. System packages change least, so they go first. The two `apt-get` commands become one step that also removes the package lists, so the lists are never stored in a layer. The dependency list is copied alone, then installed. The source comes last.

After this, a source change reruns only the last `COPY`.

choices.feedback: The text is the same, but the input to `COPY . .` is the content of the files, and one of them changed.

choices.text: Only `COPY . .`
choices.feedback: Once a step runs again, every step after it runs again. The install is below the copy.

choices.text: Both, so the dependencies are installed again
choices.feedback: The copy has a changed input, and the install comes after it, so the cached install cannot be used.

questions.prompt: What goes wrong?

choices.text: The install uses a package list that is three months old
choices.feedback: The first line is unchanged, so its cached layer is reused. The changed second line runs against old lists and may ask for package versions that no longer exist. One `RUN` with both commands keeps them in step.

choices.text: The build fails because `apt-get update` runs twice
choices.feedback: It does not run at all. Its layer comes from the cache.

choices.text: Nothing, the cache makes the build faster
choices.feedback: It is faster, and wrong. The lists and the install were made at different times.

lessons.title: Start and stop cleanly
lessons.intro: A container is one main process. How that process is started decides how it can be given arguments, and how it is started also decides whether it can be stopped cleanly. This module covers the two instructions that set the start command, the two ways of writing them, and what happens when Docker asks a container to stop.

steps.title: The main process
steps.text:
When a container starts, Docker runs one command inside it. That is the **main process**. Inside the container it has process number 1, written PID 1.

Everything about the container's life hangs on it. The container is running while PID 1 is alive. Its output is what `docker logs` shows. Its exit code becomes the container's exit code. When it ends, the container stops, even if other processes were still working.

The image decides what the command is, with two instructions: `CMD` and `ENTRYPOINT`.

steps.title: CMD and ENTRYPOINT
steps.text:
- `CMD` sets a **default** that is easy to replace. Anything typed after the image name in `docker run` replaces it entirely.
- `ENTRYPOINT` sets a **fixed** start. Anything typed after the image name is added to it as arguments.
- With both, the entrypoint is the program and `CMD` supplies its default arguments.

Use `CMD` alone for a service, where the image has one obvious thing to run and replacing it now and then is handy. Use `ENTRYPOINT` when the image *is* a command-line tool and people will pass it arguments.

steps.title: What runs?
steps.text:
An image is built with these two lines, and then run as shown.

```dockerfile
ENTRYPOINT ["node", "cli.js"]
CMD ["--help"]
```

```bash
docker run tool list --all
```

steps.title: Two ways to write a command
steps.text:
`CMD`, `ENTRYPOINT` and `RUN` can each be written in two forms, and the difference matters.

The **exec form** is a list in square brackets. Docker starts that program directly, with those arguments. The program is PID 1.

The **shell form** is a plain line of text. Docker hands it to a shell, as `/bin/sh -c "..."`. The shell is PID 1 and your program is its child.

The shell form is convenient, because variables and `&&` work in it. For the command a container starts with, it has a cost that the next step explains. Prefer the exec form for `CMD` and `ENTRYPOINT`.

steps.title: How a container is asked to stop
steps.text:
`docker stop` does not pull the plug. It sends PID 1 a polite request to end, the signal named `SIGTERM`. A well behaved service responds by finishing the requests it is handling, closing its connections and exiting.

Docker waits 10 seconds. If the process is still alive, Docker sends `SIGKILL`, which the process cannot catch. It ends at once, in the middle of whatever it was doing.

Now recall the shell form. The request goes to PID 1, which is the shell. A shell does not pass the request on to its child. The service never hears it, keeps running, and is killed 10 seconds later.

Some shells step aside when the line is one plain command, so you will not see this in every image. Do not depend on it. The exec form behaves the same way everywhere.

steps.title: Ten seconds, every time
steps.text: A team notices that every deploy of their service pauses for exactly ten seconds, and that some requests fail during it. This is what they see.

steps.title: PID 1 has to listen
steps.text:
Writing the command in exec form puts your program at PID 1, where it receives the request. It still has to act on it.

PID 1 is treated specially by the kernel: a signal that the process has not chosen to handle is ignored, where any other process would be ended by it. So a program that does nothing about `SIGTERM` behaves just like the shell did.

There are two fixes. The better one is for the program to handle `SIGTERM`: stop accepting work, finish what is in progress, exit. The other is `docker run --init`, which puts a tiny helper at PID 1 that forwards signals to your program.

When an image starts through a wrapper script, end the script with `exec` so that the program replaces the script as PID 1.

steps.title: Exit codes
steps.text:
When the main process ends, its exit code is recorded and shown by `docker ps -a`. A few values come up again and again.

| Code | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| 0 | The program ended normally. |
| 1, or another small number | The program reported an error. Read its logs. |
| 125 | Docker itself could not start the container. |
| 126 | The command was found and could not be executed. |
| 127 | The command was not found in the image. |
| 137 | Ended by `SIGKILL` (128 + 9): a stop that timed out, or out of memory. |
| 143 | Ended by `SIGTERM` (128 + 15) without handling it. |

The module on debugging returns to these.

steps.title: Exercise: two images
steps.text:
Write the start instructions for each image, and nothing else.

1. A web service started with `node server.js`. During an incident, an operator sometimes needs to start a shell in the same image.
2. A backup tool, `backup`, that is always given a subcommand such as `backup run` or `backup list`. With no subcommand it should print its help.

3. Then explain what is wrong with `CMD node server.js`.

steps.title: One possible answer
steps.text:
1. `CMD ["node", "server.js"]`. With only a `CMD`, the operator can run `docker run --rm -it tracker:1.4.2 sh` and the shell replaces the default.
2. `ENTRYPOINT ["backup"]` with `CMD ["--help"]`. `docker run backup-tool list` runs `backup list`, and `docker run backup-tool` runs `backup --help`.
3. It is the shell form. A shell becomes PID 1, the service never receives the stop request, and every stop waits ten seconds and ends in a kill. Square brackets fix it.

choices.text: `node cli.js list --all`
choices.feedback: The entrypoint stays. The words after the image name replace the `CMD`, so `--help` is dropped.

choices.text: `node cli.js --help list --all`
choices.feedback: Arguments given at run time replace the `CMD`. They are not added after it.

questions.prompt: What is the cause?

choices.text: The service never receives the stop request
choices.feedback: The command is in shell form, so a shell is PID 1 and does not forward `SIGTERM`. Docker waits its ten seconds and kills everything, which gives exit code 137.

choices.text: The service needs more than ten seconds to finish
choices.feedback: It could be given longer, but it is not finishing anything. It was never told to stop.

choices.text: The container ran out of memory
choices.feedback: Memory also gives 137, but it would not happen exactly ten seconds after every stop.

lessons.title: Configure a container
lessons.intro: An image is built once and run in many places: on a laptop, on a test server, in production. The places differ in their database address, their log level and their passwords. This module covers how one image gets different settings in each place, which settings belong to the build, and why a secret must never be part of an image. The advice on secrets is general guidance. Your organization's own security policy decides what is required where you work.

steps.title: One image, many places
steps.text:
It is tempting to build one image for testing and another for production, each with its settings inside. Then the thing you tested is not the thing you run.

The better rule is: **build one image, and give it its settings when it starts.** The image holds what is the same everywhere. The differences come from outside, in one of three ways.

- **Environment variables**, for single values.
- **Files** placed into the container when it starts, for whole configuration files.
- **Arguments** after the image name, for a tool's options.

steps.title: Environment variables
steps.text:
An environment variable is a named value that a process can read. Docker sets them in three ways.

- `ENV NAME=value` in the Dockerfile stores a **default** in the image.
- `-e NAME=value` on `docker run` sets a value for that container.
- `--env-file settings.env` reads many `NAME=value` lines from a file.

A value given at run time wins over the image's default. So use `ENV` for sensible defaults, such as the port, and leave anything that differs per place to run time.

steps.title: Which value wins?
steps.text:
The Dockerfile contains `ENV PORT=3000`. The container is started with:

```bash
docker run -e PORT=8080 tracker:1.4.2
```

steps.title: ARG is for the build
steps.text:
`ARG` looks like `ENV` and does a different job. It declares a value that exists **only while the image is being built**. You supply it with `--build-arg`.

| | `ARG` | `ENV` |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Available to `RUN` during the build | Yes | Yes |
| Present in the running container | No | Yes |
| Set from the command line | `docker build --build-arg` | `docker run -e` |
| Good for | Versions and options of the build | Settings of the program |

A typical use is choosing the version of the base image, or stamping the image with the version being built. An `ARG` is not hidden: the value is recorded in the image's history.

steps.title: Secrets do not go in images
steps.text:
A password, an API key or a private key must never be built into an image. An image is copied to registries, build servers and laptops, and everyone who can pull it can read all of it.

Every one of these puts a secret in the image for good:

- `ENV DB_PASSWORD=...` is shown by `docker inspect` and `docker history`.
- `ARG` with `--build-arg` is recorded in the history.
- `COPY .env .` stores the file in a layer, and deleting it later does not remove it.

Supply secrets when the container starts. An environment variable set at run time is common and acceptable in many places. A file placed into the container is better, because environment variables are shown to anyone who can run `docker inspect` and are easily printed into logs. The modules on Compose and on privilege show the file approach.

steps.title: A password passed through the build
steps.text: A build script and a Dockerfile, from a project that wanted to avoid writing the password in the file.

steps.title: Whole files
steps.text:
Some programs are configured by a file. You can keep one image and place a different file into each container when it starts, read-only.

```bash
docker run -d \
  -v ./tracker.conf:/etc/tracker/tracker.conf:ro \
  tracker:1.4.2
```

The part before the colon is a file on the host. The part after it is where the container sees that file. `:ro` stops the container from changing it. The module on storage covers this mechanism properly.

Choose variables for a handful of values, and a file when there is structure or there are dozens of them.

steps.title: Say what the image expects
steps.text:
Configuration from outside can be missing or wrong, so make that easy to notice.

- **Check at start.** If a required setting is missing, the program should say which one and exit with an error. A container that starts and fails on the first request is much harder to diagnose.
- **List the settings.** Put the names, meanings and defaults in the project's README, and ship an example file with invented values.
- **Never print secret values.** Log that a setting is present, not what it is.

steps.title: Exercise: where does each value go?
steps.text:
For each value, choose one: a build argument, a default in the image, a setting given at run time, or a secret given at run time.

1. The version of the runtime the image is built on.
2. The port the service listens on inside the container, almost always 3000.
3. The address of the database.
4. The database password.
5. The log level, usually `info`, sometimes `debug` on one server.
6. The version number of the build, shown on the service's status page.

steps.title: One possible answer
steps.text:
1. **Build argument.** It selects the base image and means nothing once the image exists.
2. **Default in the image.** `ENV PORT=3000`. It is the same nearly everywhere and can still be overridden.
3. **Run time.** It differs in every place.
4. **Secret at run time.** Never in the Dockerfile, never a build argument.
5. **Default in the image**, `ENV LOG_LEVEL=info`, overridden with `-e LOG_LEVEL=debug` on the one server.
6. **Build argument copied into an `ENV`.** The value is known only to the build, and the running program needs to read it. This is the one case where the two are used together, and it is safe because a version number is not a secret.

choices.text: Only someone with access to the build server

choices.feedback: The `ENV` line stores the value in the image, where `docker inspect` shows it, and the build argument is recorded in the history as well.

lessons.title: Keep data
lessons.intro: Containers are meant to be thrown away and replaced. Data is not. This module covers where a container's files really live, what is lost when a container is removed, and the three ways to keep data somewhere that outlives it.

steps.title: The writable layer
steps.text:
An image is read-only, and yet a program in a container can create and change files. It can because Docker gives every container a thin **writable layer** on top of the image's layers.

Everything the container writes goes there. When it changes a file that came from the image, the file is first copied up into the writable layer, and the copy is changed.

The writable layer belongs to that one container. It survives a stop and a start. It is deleted when the container is removed.

steps.title: A database with no storage set up
steps.text:
A database is started with the command below. It runs for a month and holds real data. Then it is upgraded the usual way: the container is removed and a new one is started from a newer image.

```bash
docker run -d --name db example/database:1.0
```

steps.title: Three places to put data
steps.text:
To keep data, mount storage from outside the container at the folder where the program writes. A **mount** makes outside storage appear as a folder inside. Writes to that folder skip the writable layer.

| Kind | Where the data is | Use it for |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Volume** | A storage area that Docker manages | Data the app owns: databases, uploads |
| **Bind mount** | A folder or file you choose on the host | Source code in development, config files |
| **tmpfs** | Memory only, never on disk | Scratch files that must not be kept |

Whatever is not in a mount is in the writable layer, and should be treated as disposable.

steps.title: Named volumes
steps.text:
A **volume** is the default choice for data. Give it a name and say where it appears in the container.

```bash
docker run -d --name db \
  -v tracker-data:/var/lib/postgresql/data \
  postgres:17
```

The name comes before the colon and the folder inside the container after it. Docker creates the volume the first time it is used. Removing the container leaves the volume alone, and a new container given the same volume finds the same data.

The folder must be the one the program actually writes to. An image's documentation says which it is.

steps.title: Bind mounts
steps.text:
A **bind mount** makes a folder or file from the host appear in the container. The left side is a path, not a name, which is how Docker tells the two apart.

Both sides see the same files at the same moment. That makes bind mounts ideal in development: edit the source on your machine and the container sees the change with no rebuild.

They have two costs. The container depends on a path existing on that particular host, so the setup is less portable. And the container can change or delete your files, so add `:ro` whenever it only needs to read.

steps.title: A volume that kept nothing
steps.text: This database was given a volume, and its data still disappeared when the container was replaced. PostgreSQL stores its data in `/var/lib/postgresql/data`.

steps.title: What a mount hides
steps.text:
A mount covers whatever the image had at that folder. Two cases surprise people.

- An **empty named volume** is filled first: Docker copies the image's files at that folder into the new volume. So the first start works as expected.
- A **bind mount** is never filled. If the host folder is empty, the container sees an empty folder, and the image's files there are hidden.

The classic example is mounting your project folder over `/app` in development. The dependencies installed into `/app` during the build vanish from view, because your host folder has none. The module on Compose shows a tidy way to handle it.

steps.title: A volume is yours to look after
steps.text:
A volume is not a backup. It is one copy of the data on one machine.

- **Back it up.** A throwaway container can mount the volume and write an archive to a host folder, as below. For a database, prefer the database's own dump tool, which gives a consistent copy while it is running.
- **Remove it deliberately.** `docker volume rm` deletes one volume and `docker volume prune` deletes those no container uses. Both are permanent.
- **Keep containers stateless.** If every piece of data that matters is in a volume, any container can be removed and replaced without thought. That is the goal.

steps.title: Exercise: where should it live?
steps.text:
The tracker has these kinds of data. For each, choose a volume, a bind mount, tmpfs, or nothing at all, and give a reason.

1. The database's files.
2. Pictures that users upload.
3. The source code, while a developer is working on it.
4. A configuration file written by the operations team.
5. Temporary files made while resizing a picture.
6. The service's log output.

steps.title: One possible answer
steps.text:
1. **Volume.** It is the application's own data and must outlive every container.
2. **Volume.** The same reason. On several servers it would move to shared storage, which is outside this course.
3. **Bind mount.** The developer edits on the host and the container must see each change.
4. **Bind mount, read-only.** The file is managed on the host and the container only reads it.
5. **tmpfs, or nothing.** They are worthless a second later. The writable layer is fine, and tmpfs keeps them off the disk.
6. **Nothing.** Write logs to the program's output. Docker collects them, and `docker logs` shows them. A log file inside the container grows unseen in the writable layer.

lessons.title: Connect containers
lessons.intro: A container has its own network, separate from the host's. That is why a service can be running and still unreachable. This module covers letting the outside in by publishing a port, letting containers find each other by name, and the most common confusion of all: what `localhost` means inside a container.

steps.title: A container has its own network
steps.text:
Each container gets its own network address and its own set of ports. Port 3000 in one container has nothing to do with port 3000 in another, or with port 3000 on the host. Ten containers can all listen on port 3000 without conflict.

The other side of that privacy is that nothing outside can reach a container's ports by default. A service listening on port 3000 inside a container is, at first, reachable only from inside that container.

There are two ways in. **Publishing** a port opens it to the host and beyond. A shared **network** lets chosen containers talk to each other.

steps.title: Publish a port
steps.text:
`-p` connects a port on the host to a port in the container. The host port is written first.

```bash
docker run -d --name web -p 8080:3000 tracker:1.4.2
```

Requests to port 8080 on the host are passed to port 3000 in the container. The two numbers need not match, and the host port must be free.

- `-p 8080:3000` accepts connections from any machine that can reach the host.
- `-p 127.0.0.1:8080:3000` accepts them only from the host itself.

`EXPOSE` in a Dockerfile publishes nothing. It records which port the program uses, for people and tools to read.

steps.title: Which address?
steps.text: A container is started with `-p 8080:3000`. The service inside listens on port 3000. You open a browser on the same machine.

steps.title: Listen on every interface
steps.text:
One more thing has to be right, and it is inside the program. A service chooses which network interface to listen on.

If it listens on `127.0.0.1`, it accepts only connections that start **inside the same container**. Traffic arriving through a published port comes in from outside the container, and is refused.

A service in a container must listen on `0.0.0.0`, which means every interface. Many frameworks listen on `127.0.0.1` by default when run in development mode. A published port that refuses every connection is very often this.

steps.title: Containers that talk to each other
steps.text:
The tracker needs to reach its database. Put both containers on a network you create, and each can reach the other **by container name**. Docker runs a small name service on such networks.

Two details matter.

- Use the **container's** port, 5432 here. Published ports are for traffic from the host. Between containers on one network they play no part, and the database needs no `-p` at all.
- Use a network you created. The default network that containers join when you name none has no lookup by name.

steps.title: Connection refused
steps.text: The web service and the database run as two containers on the same network. The web service was given the settings below, which worked on the developer's laptop before Docker was used. Now it logs `connection refused`.

steps.title: Out to the world, and back to the host
steps.text:
Outbound traffic works without any setup. A container can reach the internet and other machines as the host can.

Reaching a service that runs **on the host itself**, outside Docker, needs a name for the host. Inside a container, `localhost` is the container. Docker Desktop provides the name `host.docker.internal` for this. On Linux, add it yourself:

```bash
docker run --add-host=host.docker.internal:host-gateway ...
```

This is useful in development, for example when the database runs directly on your laptop.

steps.title: Publish as little as you can
steps.text:
Every published port is a door into the host. Open only the ones that are needed.

- **Publish the front door only.** The web service is published. The database is reached over the shared network and is published nowhere.
- **Bind to `127.0.0.1` in development.** A plain `-p 5432:5432` offers the database to everyone on the same network as your laptop.
- **Check from outside.** On Linux, Docker opens published ports with its own firewall rules, and those can take effect ahead of the rules of a host firewall tool. Test from another machine before trusting that a port is closed.

steps.title: Exercise: three containers
steps.text:
The tracker now has three containers: `web` (port 3000), `db` (port 5432) and `cache` (port 6379). Users reach the web service on port 80 of the server. Only `web` talks to `db` and `cache`.

1. Which ports do you publish, and how?
2. What address does `web` use for the database, and for the cache?
3. A developer wants to open the database with a tool on their own laptop while developing. What do you add, on the laptop only?

steps.title: One possible answer
steps.text:
1. One port: `-p 80:3000` on `web`. Nothing on `db` or `cache`.
2. `db:5432` and `cache:6379`, with all three containers on one created network. The names are the container names and the ports are the containers' own.
3. `-p 127.0.0.1:5432:5432` on `db`, in the development setup only. The tool on the laptop connects to `localhost:5432`, and no other machine can.

The pattern to remember: names and container ports between containers, published ports only for what must come in from outside.

lessons.title: Describe an app with Compose
lessons.intro: By now, starting the tracker takes a network, a volume and two long `docker run` commands that must be typed in the right order. Docker Compose replaces them with one file that describes the whole application, and one command that makes it so. This module covers reading and writing that file and the handful of commands used with it.

steps.title: One file for the whole application
steps.text:
**Docker Compose** reads a file named `compose.yaml` that describes an application as a set of **services**. A service is one container image together with how to run it: its ports, its settings, its storage.

The file is a description, not a script. It says what should exist. `docker compose up` compares that with what does exist and creates, replaces or leaves each piece as needed.

The file lives in the project and is committed with the code. A new team member starts the whole application with one command and no setup page.

steps.title: Reading the file
steps.text:
Each entry under `services` uses ideas from earlier modules under a new spelling.

| In the file | Same as | Module |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `image:` | The image name in `docker run` | Images |
| `build:` | `docker build` on that folder | Dockerfile |
| `ports:` | `-p host:container` | Network |
| `environment:` | `-e NAME=value` | Config |
| `volumes:` | `-v name:/path` or `-v ./path:/path` | Storage |
| `depends_on:` | Start the named service first | The next module |

Named volumes are also listed once at the top level, under `volumes:`, so that Compose creates them.

Compose makes one network for the application and puts every service on it. Each service can reach the others **by service name**.

steps.title: Finding the database
steps.text: In the file you just read, the `web` service has to connect to PostgreSQL in the `db` service.

steps.title: The commands
steps.text:
Run these in the folder that holds `compose.yaml`.

| Command | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `docker compose up -d` | Creates and starts everything, in the background. |
| `docker compose ps` | Lists the application's containers. |
| `docker compose logs -f web` | Follows one service's output. |
| `docker compose exec web sh` | Opens a shell in a running service. |
| `docker compose up -d --build` | Rebuilds images, then replaces what changed. |
| `docker compose down` | Stops and removes the containers and the network. |

`down` keeps named volumes, so the data is still there at the next `up`. Running `up` again after editing the file replaces only the services whose description changed.

Compose names everything after the **project**, which is the folder's name unless you say otherwise. The volume `db-data` in a folder named `tracker` is really `tracker_db-data`.

steps.title: A cleanup script
steps.text: A team's reset script for their shared test server. The server's database holds test data that took a week to prepare.

steps.title: Variables in the file
steps.text:
A Compose file can take values from the environment with `${NAME}`. Add `:-` and a default for when the variable is not set.

Compose also reads a file named `.env` beside `compose.yaml` and uses its lines for this substitution. That makes `.env` the place for per-machine choices such as which port to publish.

Two features have similar names and do different jobs.

- `.env` supplies values **to the Compose file**, for `${...}`.
- `env_file:` under a service passes the lines of a file **into the container** as environment variables.

A value in `.env` reaches a container only if the Compose file passes it on.

steps.title: Secrets as files
steps.text:
The module on configuration said that a secret is better supplied as a file than as an environment variable. Compose has a section for this.

A secret listed at the top level is taken from a file on the host. A service that names it sees its content at `/run/secrets/<name>` inside the container. Many images accept a variable ending in `_FILE` that points to such a file, as the official PostgreSQL image does.

The secret file itself stays out of version control and out of the image. As before, this is general guidance. Where you work, the organization's own policy on storing secrets applies.

steps.title: Compose in development
steps.text:
The same file serves day-to-day development with small additions.

- **A bind mount of the source** lets the container see edits at once. Compose reads a second file, `compose.override.yaml`, when it exists, and merges it over the first. Put development-only additions there.
- **`docker compose watch`** copies changed files into the running container, or rebuilds when a file such as the dependency list changes. It avoids the bind mount's habit of hiding files that the image installed.

Keep the main file as the description of the real application, and the extras for development in the override file.

steps.title: Exercise: add a worker
steps.text:
The tracker gets a background worker that sends email. It is the **same image** as `web`, started with a different command: `node worker.js`. It needs the same database settings, listens on no port, and must be started along with everything else.

1. Write the `worker` service.
2. Say what you did not include, and why.
3. Give the one command that shows only the worker's output.

steps.text:
1. The service is below. `command:` replaces the image's `CMD` for this service, which is how one image can do two jobs.
2. No `ports:`, because nothing connects to the worker. It makes outgoing connections only. The `build:` and `image:` lines are the same as in `web`, so that both services use one image.
3. `docker compose logs -f worker`.

The two services repeat their database settings. That is acceptable at this size. Larger files share them with an `env_file`.

lessons.title: Start in order and stay up
lessons.intro: An application made of several containers has to start in a workable order, recover when a part fails, and not take the whole machine down when a part misbehaves. This module covers health checks, waiting for a dependency to be ready, restart policies and resource limits.

steps.title: Started is not ready
steps.text:
`depends_on` in its short form makes Compose start the database container before the web container. It does not wait for the database to be **ready**.

A database needs several seconds after its process starts before it accepts connections. The web service starts a moment later, tries to connect, and fails.

Docker knows when a process has started. It cannot know by itself when a program is ready to do its job. You have to tell it how to find out.

steps.title: Health checks
steps.text:
A **health check** is a command that Docker runs inside the container at intervals. Exit code 0 means healthy. Anything else means not healthy.

| Setting | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `test` | The command to run. |
| `interval` | How long to wait between checks. |
| `timeout` | How long one check may take before it counts as failed. |
| `retries` | How many failures in a row make the container unhealthy. |
| `start_period` | Time at the start during which failures do not count. |

A container with a health check is `starting`, then `healthy` or `unhealthy`. `docker ps` shows the state.

The command must exist in the image. A good check asks the program a real question, such as whether it accepts a connection, and is cheap enough to run every few seconds.

steps.title: Wait for healthy
steps.text:
With a health check in place, `depends_on` can use its long form and name a condition.

- `service_started` is the default: the container has been started.
- `service_healthy` waits until the health check passes.
- `service_completed_successfully` waits until the container has finished with exit code 0. It suits a one-off job that must run first, such as updating the database's tables.

steps.title: The short form
steps.text:
A Compose file says this, and the `db` service has no health check.

```yaml
  web:
    depends_on:
      - db
```

steps.title: It can still fail later
steps.text:
Start order solves the first minute. It does nothing about the rest of the application's life. A database can restart at three in the morning, long after every `depends_on` was satisfied.

So the real fix belongs in the program: **when a connection fails, wait a little and try again.** A service that retries does not care which container started first.

Use health checks and conditions to make a clean start likely. Do not use them as a reason to skip retrying.

steps.title: Restart policies
steps.text:
A restart policy tells Docker what to do when a container's main process ends.

| Policy | Restarts when |
| --- | --- |
| `no` | Never. This is the default. |
| `on-failure` | The exit code is not 0. |
| `always` | It ends for any reason, and when the Docker daemon starts. |
| `unless-stopped` | As `always`, except after you stopped it yourself. |

`unless-stopped` suits most long-running services. They come back after a crash and after the machine reboots, and stay down when you stop them on purpose.

Docker waits a little longer before each new attempt. And note what a policy does not do: Docker by itself does not restart a container for being **unhealthy**. It restarts one only when the main process ends.

steps.title: Up, down, up, down
steps.text: After a change to its settings, a service looks like this. Each time anyone checks, the uptime is a few seconds.

steps.title: Limits
steps.text:
With no limit, one container can use all of the host's memory and processor time, and starve every other container on the machine.

- A **memory limit** is a hard cap. A container that goes over it is killed by the kernel. It ends with exit code 137, and `docker inspect` reports `OOMKilled: true`.
- A **CPU limit** is a throttle. The container is slowed down and is not killed.

Set a memory limit somewhat above what the service needs in normal use. A leak then takes down one container, which its restart policy brings back, and the rest of the machine carries on.

steps.title: Exercise: a start that works
steps.text:
The tracker has three services: `db`, a one-off `migrate` job that updates the database's tables and exits, and `web`.

1. Describe the order they must become ready in.
2. Write the `depends_on` section of `migrate` and of `web`.
3. Choose a restart policy for each of the three, with a reason.

steps.title: One possible answer
steps.text:
1. `db` must be healthy, then `migrate` must finish successfully, then `web` may start.
2. The sections are below. `web` waits for both. Waiting for `migrate` alone would be enough for the order, and naming `db` too states the real dependency.
3. `db` and `web`: `unless-stopped`, so they return after a crash or a reboot. `migrate`: `no`. It is meant to run once and end. With `always` it would run again and again for ever. If it fails, a person should read why.

questions.prompt: What does this guarantee when `web` starts?

choices.text: That the `db` container has been started
choices.feedback: The short form only orders the starts. The database may still be seconds away from accepting connections.

choices.text: That the database accepts connections
choices.feedback: That needs a health check on `db` and the condition `service_healthy`.

choices.text: Nothing about order at all
choices.feedback: It does order the starts. It does not wait for readiness.

questions.prompt: What is the best next step?

choices.text: Change the policy to `unless-stopped`
choices.feedback: The policy is doing its job. The program ends with an error each time it starts.

choices.text: Read the container's logs
choices.feedback: Exit code 1 means the program reported an error, and it does so at every start. The logs say what the new settings broke. Restarting cannot fix a wrong setting.

choices.text: Give the container more memory
choices.feedback: Running out of memory gives 137. This is exit code 1, an error the program reported itself.

timeline.code:
time  0s      1s      2s      3s      4s      5s      6s
        |-------|-------|-------|-------|-------|-------|

  db    [ process started .......... preparing .... ][ ready ]
                                                     ^
  web      [ started ][ connects --> refused ][ exits with an error ]
            ^
            depends_on (short form) waited only for this

services:
  db:
    image: postgres:17.2
    healthcheck:
      # Exit code 0 when the database accepts connections.
      test: ["CMD-SHELL", "pg_isready -U postgres"]
      interval: 5s
      timeout: 3s
      retries: 5
      start_period: 10s

# $ docker compose ps
# NAME           STATUS
# tracker-db-1   Up 12 seconds (healthy)

depends.code:
services:
  web:
    image: tracker:1.4.2
    depends_on:
      db:
        condition: service_healthy

restart.code:
services:
  web:
    image: tracker:1.4.2
    restart: unless-stopped

  db:
    image: postgres:17.2
    restart: unless-stopped

# The same thing with docker run:
#   docker run -d --restart unless-stopped tracker:1.4.2

$ docker compose ps
NAME            STATUS
tracker-web-1   Restarting (1) 4 seconds ago
tracker-db-1    Up 2 hours (healthy)

# compose.yaml
  web:
    restart: always

services:
  web:
    image: tracker:1.4.2
    mem_limit: 512m     # killed if it uses more (exit code 137)
    cpus: 1.5           # slowed down beyond one and a half processors

# The same thing with docker run:
#   docker run -d --memory 512m --cpus 1.5 tracker:1.4.2
#
# Watch what containers actually use:
#   docker stats

services:
  db:
    image: postgres:17.2
    restart: unless-stopped
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD-SHELL", "pg_isready -U postgres"]
      interval: 5s
      retries: 5

  migrate:
    image: tracker:1.4.2
    command: ["node", "migrate.js"]
    restart: "no"
    depends_on:
      db:
        condition: service_healthy

  web:
    image: tracker:1.4.2
    restart: unless-stopped
    depends_on:
      db:
        condition: service_healthy
      migrate:
        condition: service_completed_successfully

lessons.title: Build small images
lessons.intro: The first Dockerfile in this course produced a working image that was larger than it needed to be. This module covers why size matters, how a multi-stage build ships only what the program needs to run, and how to choose a base image.

steps.title: Why size matters
steps.text:
A large image costs you in three ways.

- **Time.** Every build pushes it and every server pulls it. A deploy, a rollback and a new server all wait for the download.
- **Space.** Registries and servers keep many versions.
- **Risk.** Every tool and library in the image is something that can have a security flaw and must be kept patched, whether your program uses it or not.

The third matters most. A small image has less in it to go wrong.

steps.title: What you build with is not what you run with
steps.text:
Building a program needs things that running it does not: compilers, build tools, test libraries, the source in its original form.

A single-stage Dockerfile installs all of that to do the build, and then ships it. Cleaning up at the end does not help, because the files remain in earlier layers.

What is needed is two separate environments: one to build in, and a clean one that receives only the result.

steps.title: Multi-stage builds
steps.text:
A Dockerfile may contain more than one `FROM`. Each starts a new **stage** with a fresh set of files. A stage can be named with `AS`.

`COPY --from=<stage>` copies files out of an earlier stage into the current one. That is the only thing that crosses from one stage to the next.

**The image is the last stage.** Earlier stages are used during the build and then left behind. Their tools and layers are not part of what you ship.

steps.title: What is in the final image?
steps.text: In the multi-stage file you just read, the first stage runs `npm ci`, which installs every dependency including the build tools.

steps.title: Choosing a base image
steps.text:
The final stage's `FROM` sets the floor for the image's size and contents.

| Base | Contains | Consider |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Full, such as `node:24` | A whole distribution with build tools | Convenient for a build stage. Large to ship. |
| Slim, such as `node:24-slim` | The runtime and a minimal distribution | A sound default for the final stage. |
| Alpine, such as `node:24-alpine` | The runtime on a very small distribution | Smallest with a shell. Uses a different system library, and some prebuilt packages do not work with it. |
| Distroless or `scratch` | The runtime only, or nothing at all | No shell and no package manager. Smallest and hardest to look inside. |

Start with slim. Move to something smaller when you have a reason and have tested that everything still works.

steps.title: Smaller in every stage
steps.text:
A few habits help with or without stages.

- **Use `.dockerignore`**, so that a broad `COPY` cannot bring in unwanted files.
- **Install only what runs.** Leave out development dependencies in the final stage, for example with `npm ci --omit=dev`.
- **Skip suggested extras.** With `apt-get install`, add `--no-install-recommends`, and remove the package lists in the same `RUN`.
- **Do not add tools just in case.** An editor and a network toolkit in every production image are rarely used and always present. The module on debugging shows other ways to look inside.

steps.title: Where did 1.4 GB come from?
steps.text: The layers of an image built with a single stage on the full base image.

steps.title: Stages are also targets
steps.text:
Stages have a second use. `docker build --target <stage>` stops at the named stage and produces an image of it.

That lets one Dockerfile serve several purposes: a `build` stage with every tool, in which the tests can run on a build server, and a final stage for shipping. Both come from the same file, so they cannot drift apart.

steps.title: Exercise: plan the stages
steps.text:
A service is written in a language that compiles to a single executable file. Compiling needs the language's toolchain, which is 900 MB. The executable is 20 MB and needs nothing else to run except the certificates used to check secure connections.

1. How many stages, and what does each do?
2. What does the final stage start from?
3. What crosses between the stages?
4. Roughly how large is the image you ship?

steps.title: One possible answer
steps.text:
1. Two. A `build` stage from the toolchain's image compiles the program. A final stage holds the result.
2. A minimal base that has certificates and little else: a distroless image, or a slim distribution if a shell is wanted for looking around.
3. One file, the executable, with `COPY --from=build`.
4. A little over 20 MB plus the base, against more than 900 MB for a single stage.

The same plan fits any language. Only the first stage and the files that are copied across change.

questions.prompt: Are the build tools in the image that is shipped?

choices.text: Yes, every stage is part of the image
choices.feedback: Only the last stage is the image. Earlier stages are discarded once the build ends.

choices.text: Yes, but hidden in a lower layer
choices.feedback: That is what happens in a single stage. A new `FROM` starts from a fresh set of files, with no layers from the stage before.

choices.text: No, only what the final stage copied or installed
choices.feedback: The final stage starts from a clean base. It holds the build output it copied across and the run-time dependencies it installed itself.

questions.prompt: Which single change saves the most?

choices.text: A final stage built from the slim base
choices.feedback: The base accounts for about 1.1 GB of the total. A final stage from the slim base, about 230 MB, removes most of it at once and leaves the development dependencies behind as well.

choices.text: Adding `.dockerignore`
choices.feedback: Useful, but the source layer is only 61 MB.

choices.text: Joining the `RUN` lines into one
choices.feedback: That saves almost nothing here. No layer is deleting files left by another.

two-rooms.code:
STAGE 1: build                          STAGE 2: what you ship
  +-----------------------------+         +-------------------------+
  | full base image             |         | slim base image         |
  | compilers and build tools   |         |                         |
  | development dependencies    |         | run-time dependencies   |
  | source code                 |         |                         |
  |                             |  COPY   |                         |
  | build output  --------------+-------> | build output            |
  +-----------------------------+ --from  +-------------------------+
        thrown away after the build              this is the image

multi.code:
# ---- Stage 1: build ----
FROM node:24.11.1 AS build
WORKDIR /app
COPY package.json package-lock.json ./
RUN npm ci
COPY . .
RUN npm run build          # writes the result to /app/dist

# ---- Stage 2: the image that is shipped ----
FROM node:24.11.1-slim
WORKDIR /app
COPY package.json package-lock.json ./
RUN npm ci --omit=dev
COPY --from=build /app/dist ./dist

CMD ["node", "dist/server.js"]
