lessons.title: Run with less privilege
lessons.intro: A container limits what a program can see. It is not a strong wall. This module covers the habits that reduce what a container can do if the program inside it is broken into, and what you are trusting when you build on someone else's image. It is general guidance and not a complete security standard. Where you work, your organization's own security policy and review decide what is required.

steps.title: What can go wrong
steps.text:
Assume that one day the program in a container will be taken over, through a flaw in its own code or in a library. The question is what the attacker can do next.

Two facts from the first module set the stakes. Containers share the host's kernel, so the boundary is thinner than a virtual machine's. And unless you say otherwise, the process in a container runs as **root**, the all-powerful user, which is by default the same user as root on the host.

Root inside a container is still restricted by the container. A mistake in the setup or a flaw in the kernel can remove that restriction. So the aim is to give the program as little power as it can work with. Each habit below removes something an attacker would otherwise have.

steps.title: Do not run as root
steps.text:
The most valuable single change is to run the program as an ordinary user. The `USER` instruction sets the user for the rest of the Dockerfile and for the container.

Many official images ship a suitable user. The Node.js image has one named `node`. Where none exists, create one in a `RUN` step.

Do the steps that need root first: installing system packages, creating folders. Then switch. Files that the program must write to need to belong to that user, which `COPY --chown` arranges.

An ordinary user cannot install packages, change system files or read other users' files. Most services need none of those.

steps.title: Who is it running as?
steps.text:
You run this against a production container, and it prints `root`.

```bash
docker exec web whoami
```

steps.title: Take away what is not used
steps.text:
Docker can remove more, one option at a time.

- **A read-only file system.** The container cannot change its own files. Give it a memory-backed scratch folder for the few places it must write.
- **No capabilities.** Root's power is divided into named pieces called capabilities, and Docker grants a container a default set. Most services need none. Drop them all and add back only what proves necessary.
- **No new privileges.** This stops a process from gaining more power than it started with.
- **Limits.** The memory and CPU limits from the module on health stop one container from exhausting the host.

And never use `--privileged` for an application. It switches off nearly all of the isolation.

steps.title: The Docker socket
steps.text:
The Docker daemon is controlled through a file, `/var/run/docker.sock`. Whoever can write to that file can tell the daemon to do anything, including starting a new container with the whole host disk mounted inside it.

So access to the socket is, in effect, root on the host. Two consequences follow.

- **Do not mount the socket into a container** unless the container's job is to manage Docker, and then treat that container as fully trusted.
- **Membership of the `docker` group on a server is administrator access.** Grant it as carefully as you would a root password.

steps.title: Three settings
steps.text: Part of a Compose file from a project that "had permission problems" and "needed to reach the database from a laptop".

steps.title: Trust what you build on
steps.text:
Your image is mostly other people's files: the base image and every dependency. Their flaws become yours.

- **Choose the publisher.** Prefer official images and the software maker's own. Read how any other image is built.
- **Pin what you use.** A specific version, and a digest for production, so that nothing changes without a decision.
- **Rebuild regularly.** Pinning keeps out surprises and also keeps out fixes. Update the pinned versions and rebuild on a schedule, not only when the code changes.
- **Scan.** An image scanner lists known flaws in the packages an image contains. Docker's own is `docker scout cves <image>`, and registries and build systems offer others. Run one in the build, and decide in advance which findings stop a release.
- **Ship less.** Everything the last module removed is something that no longer needs scanning or patching.

steps.title: Secrets during a build
steps.text:
Sometimes the build itself needs a secret, for example a token to download private dependencies. The module on configuration ruled out `ARG`, `ENV` and `COPY`, because each leaves the value in the image.

A **secret mount** is the safe way. The secret is given to `docker build` from outside. It appears as a file for the length of one `RUN` step and is stored in no layer.

Secrets that the program needs while running are supplied when the container starts, as a file under `/run/secrets`, as the module on Compose showed.

steps.title: Exercise: review a service
steps.text:
A web service is described this way. List what you would change, most important first.

```yaml
  web:
    image: tracker
    user: root
    ports:
      - "80:3000"
      - "9229:9229"   # debugger
    environment:
      API_KEY: "..."
    volumes:
      - /:/host
```

steps.title: One possible answer
steps.text:
1. **`/:/host`.** The whole host disk is mounted into the container, writable. Anyone who takes over the program owns the server. Remove it, and mount only the specific folder that is needed, read-only if possible.
2. **`user: root`.** Run as an ordinary user.
3. **The debugger port.** A debugger lets whoever connects run code inside the process, and this one is open to every machine that can reach the host. Remove it from anything that is not a developer's own machine.
4. **The key in the file.** Supply it as a secret file, and keep it out of version control.
5. **`image: tracker`.** It resolves to `latest`. Name a version.
6. Then add what is missing: a read-only file system, dropped capabilities, no new privileges, and a memory limit.

The order is by how much damage each allows, not by how easy it is to fix.

questions.prompt: What does that tell you?

choices.text: Nothing, containers always report root
choices.feedback: They report whichever user the process runs as. An image with a `USER` instruction reports that user.

choices.text: The service runs with more power than it needs
choices.feedback: No `USER` was set, so the service runs as root. Anyone who takes over the service gets root inside the container, which makes every other weakness more serious.

choices.text: The container has been broken into
choices.feedback: Root is the default, not a sign of an attack. It is a setting to fix.

questions.prompt: Which line is the most serious?

choices.text: `privileged: true`
choices.feedback: It removes nearly all of the container's isolation. A program taken over inside it can reach the host's devices and take control of the host. The permission problem it was hiding should be fixed by giving the right user access to the right folder.

choices.text: Publishing port 5432
choices.feedback: This exposes the database to other machines, which is bad and should be bound to `127.0.0.1` or removed. It still leaves the attacker outside the host.

choices.text: `restart: always`
choices.feedback: This is an ordinary restart policy.

user.code:
FROM node:24.11.1-slim
WORKDIR /app

# Steps that need root come first.
COPY package.json package-lock.json ./
RUN npm ci --omit=dev

# Program files belong to the ordinary user that the image provides.
COPY --chown=node:node . .

# Everything from here on, and the container, runs as that user.
USER node

CMD ["node", "server.js"]

# Where the base image has no such user, create one first:
#   RUN useradd --system --create-home app
#   USER app

harden.code:
services:
  web:
    image: tracker:1.4.2
    user: node
    read_only: true            # cannot change its own files
    tmpfs:
      - /tmp                   # a scratch folder in memory
    cap_drop:
      - ALL                    # none of root's special powers
    security_opt:
      - no-new-privileges:true
    mem_limit: 512m

# The same thing with docker run:
#   docker run -d --read-only --tmpfs /tmp --cap-drop ALL \
#     --security-opt no-new-privileges --memory 512m tracker:1.4.2

risky.code:
services:
  web:
    image: tracker:1.4.2
    privileged: true
    restart: always

  db:
    image: postgres:17.2
    ports:
      - "5432:5432"

# Dockerfile
# The token is readable at /run/secrets/npm_token during this step only.
# It is not stored in the image.
RUN --mount=type=secret,id=npm_token \
    NPM_TOKEN="$(cat /run/secrets/npm_token)" npm ci --omit=dev

# Build. The token comes from a file outside the build context.
docker build --secret id=npm_token,src=$HOME/.npm_token -t tracker:1.4.2 .

lessons.title: Tag, push and release
lessons.intro: An image on your laptop helps nobody else. This module covers getting an image to the machines that run it: pushing it to a registry, naming it so that every release can be identified, and making sure that the image that was tested is the image that runs.

steps.title: From a laptop to a server
steps.text:
The path is the same for every project.

1. **Build** the image, usually on a build server so that no one's laptop is part of the process.
2. **Push** it to a registry.
3. **Pull** it on each machine that will run it.
4. **Run** it there with that place's settings.

The registry is the meeting point. Nothing is copied from the build machine to the servers directly.

steps.title: Tag and push
steps.text:
An image's name says where it goes. To push to a registry, the image needs a name that begins with that registry's address.

`docker tag` adds a second name to an existing image. It copies nothing. The image then has two names for the same content.

`docker push` uploads it. Layers the registry already has are skipped, so pushing a new version of a familiar image sends only the layers that changed.

A registry needs to know who you are before it accepts a push. `docker login` does that, and it is something you do yourself with your own account.

steps.title: What to call a release
steps.text:
Give every build a tag that will never be used for anything else.

- **A version**, such as `1.4.2`, when the project has releases.
- **The commit identifier**, such as `git-3f2a9c8`, when it does not. It leads straight back to the exact source.

Treat these tags as permanent. Never push different content under a tag that was already used. Many registries can enforce that.

Moving tags such as `1.4` or `latest` may be offered as a convenience for people trying the image. Nothing you deploy should refer to them.

steps.title: Which image was running?
steps.text: Production runs `tracker:latest`. Every build pushes a new `latest`. On Tuesday a bad build is deployed and the team wants to go back to Monday's.

steps.title: Build once, promote the same image
steps.text:
It is common to see an image rebuilt for each environment: one build for testing, another for production. The two are different images even when the source is the same. A base tag may have moved between the builds, and a dependency may have published a new version.

Build **once**. Test that image. Then run **that same image**, by the same tag or digest, in the next environment. Moving one image forward through environments is called promotion.

This works only because settings live outside the image, as the module on configuration required. An image with production's settings built in cannot be tested anywhere else.

steps.title: Platforms
steps.text:
An image contains programs compiled for one kind of processor. The two common platforms are `linux/amd64`, used by most servers, and `linux/arm64`, used by recent Apple laptops and a growing share of servers.

By default a build targets the machine it runs on. An image built on an arm64 laptop and run on an amd64 server fails at once with the error `exec format error`.

Either build on the same kind of machine you deploy to, or name the platforms. One tag can hold a version for each, and every machine pulls the one that fits it.

steps.title: It worked on the laptop
steps.text: A developer builds and pushes an image from a new laptop. The server pulls it and the container ends immediately.

steps.title: Record where an image came from
steps.text:
Months later, someone will look at a running container and ask which source it was built from. **Labels** answer that. A label is a name and a value stored in the image.

There are standard names for the common facts: the source repository, the commit, the version and the build time. `docker inspect` shows them.

Set them from build arguments, so that the build server fills them in.

steps.title: Replace, do not repair
steps.text:
A running container is never updated in place. To release a new version, start a new container from the new image and remove the old one.

The same rule covers emergencies. Do not fix production with `docker exec` and an editor. The fix lives only in that one container's writable layer. It is lost at the next restart and nobody else knows it exists. Fix the source, build, and deploy.

Going back is then the same action as going forward: run the previous tag. Keep enough old tags in the registry for that to be possible.

steps.title: Exercise: a release
steps.text:
A team builds `tracker` from commit `3f2a9c8`, version 1.5.0, and keeps images at `registry.example.com/team/tracker`.

1. Which tags do you push for this build?
2. Which name does the production Compose file refer to?
3. The image is tested on the test server on Monday. What is deployed to production on Tuesday, and what is not done?
4. On Wednesday version 1.5.0 turns out to be faulty. What is the rollback?

steps.title: One possible answer
steps.text:
1. `registry.example.com/team/tracker:1.5.0` and `:git-3f2a9c8`. Both are permanent names for one image.
2. The version tag, `...tracker:1.5.0`, or that tag with its digest. Never `latest`.
3. The image that was tested, pulled by the same tag. It is not rebuilt for production. Only the settings differ.
4. Change the production file back to `1.4.2` and run `docker compose up -d`. The old image is still in the registry, so going back takes one pull and one restart.

questions.prompt: What is the problem?

choices.text: Nothing, they can pull `latest` again
choices.feedback: `latest` now points at Tuesday's bad build. Pulling it again fetches the same thing.

choices.text: Old images are deleted when a tag moves
choices.feedback: The old image may well still exist in the registry. The trouble is that it no longer has a name anyone can use.

choices.text: No name points at Monday's image any more
choices.feedback: Each push moved `latest`, so Monday's image has no tag. A permanent tag per build would have made the rollback a one-line change.

questions.prompt: What is the cause?

choices.text: The image was built for a different kind of processor
choices.feedback: `exec format error` means the kernel was asked to run a program compiled for another processor type. The laptop built for arm64 and the server is amd64.

choices.text: The start command is missing from the image
choices.feedback: A missing command gives exit code 127 and the message "not found".

choices.text: The image was damaged while being pushed
choices.feedback: Layers are checked against their digests. Damaged content would be refused at the pull.

push.code:
# Build with the full name straight away ...
docker build -t registry.example.com/team/tracker:1.5.0 .

# ... or add the name to an image that already exists.
docker tag tracker:dev registry.example.com/team/tracker:1.5.0

# Upload it. You sign in to the registry yourself first (docker login).
docker push registry.example.com/team/tracker:1.5.0

# On a server:
docker pull registry.example.com/team/tracker:1.5.0

promote.code:
Rebuilding for each place: two different images

    source --build--> image A --> test         "it passed"
    source --build--> image B --> production   never tested

  Building once and promoting: one image

    source --build--> tracker:1.5.0 --> test --> staging --> production
                      (one digest)       |          |            |
                                      settings   settings     settings
                                      for test   for staging  for prod

platform.code:
# See which platform an image was built for.

lessons.title: Find out why it failed
lessons.intro: Sooner or later a container will not start, cannot be reached, or loses its data. This module gives an order in which to ask questions, the command that answers each one, and the usual causes. Nearly everything here was introduced in an earlier module. The skill is in knowing where to look first.

steps.title: Ask in order
steps.text:
Guessing is slow. Four questions, asked in the same order every time, find most problems.

1. **What state is it in?** Running, stopped, restarting, or never created.
2. **What did it say?** Its output is the program's own account of what went wrong.
3. **How did it end?** The exit code separates a program error from a kill.
4. **What does it see?** Its settings, files, mounts and network, from the inside.

Each question has one command, shown below.

steps.title: State and exit code
steps.text:
`docker ps -a` shows every container with its state. The status column holds the exit code in brackets.

`docker inspect` prints everything Docker knows about a container. It is long, so ask for one field with `--format`.

| Exit code | Usual cause | Look at |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 0 | The program finished. A service should not. | The start command |
| 1 or similar | The program reported an error. | The logs |
| 126, 127 | The command cannot be run, or is not in the image. | `CMD`, and a typing error |
| 137 | Killed: out of memory, or a stop that timed out. | `OOMKilled`, the memory limit |
| 143 | Ended by a stop request it did not handle. | Normally nothing |

steps.title: Killed
steps.text: A service runs for about an hour and then stops. `docker ps -a` shows `Exited (137)`. Nobody stopped it. `docker inspect` reports `OOMKilled: true`.

steps.title: It ends as soon as it starts
steps.text:
`docker logs` works on a stopped container, so start there. The usual causes are a missing setting, a file that is not where the program expects, or a start command with a mistake in it.

`docker exec` does not work, because nothing is running to go into. To look around, start a **new** container from the same image with a shell in place of the usual command.

If the image has no shell at all, as with a distroless base, copy files out with `docker cp`, or build and inspect the stage before the final one.

steps.title: It runs and cannot be reached
steps.text:
Work from the outside in.

1. **Is the port published?** In `docker ps`, a published port shows an arrow: `0.0.0.0:8080->3000/tcp`. A bare `3000/tcp` is not published.
2. **Is it the right container port?** The number after the arrow must be the one the program listens on.
3. **Does the program listen on every interface?** Listening on `127.0.0.1` refuses everything that comes through a published port.
4. **Does it answer from inside?** If it does, the program is fine and the problem is in steps 1 to 3.

Between two containers, check instead that both are on the same created network and that the name used is the other's container or service name.

steps.title: No arrow
steps.text: A service is running, its logs say it is listening, and the browser on the same machine cannot open `localhost:3000`.

steps.title: The data is gone, or the disk is full
steps.text:
**Data that disappeared** was almost always in a writable layer. Ask `docker inspect` which mounts the container has, and compare the mounted folder with the folder the program writes to.

**A full disk** is usually Docker's own storage: old images, stopped containers, build cache and volumes nobody uses. `docker system df` shows how much each takes.

| Command | Deletes |
| --- | --- |
| `docker container prune` | Stopped containers |
| `docker image prune` | Images with no name and no container |
| `docker builder prune` | Build cache |
| `docker volume prune` | Volumes that no container uses |
| `docker system prune` | The first three, and unused networks |

Read each list of what will be removed before you agree. A volume that no container currently uses may still hold the only copy of some data.

steps.title: Watch it happen
steps.text:
Three commands show what is going on now.

- `docker logs -f --since 10m web` follows the output, starting ten minutes back.
- `docker stats` shows the memory and processor use of each container, updated live. A number that climbs steadily towards the limit is a leak.
- `docker events` prints what Docker itself does: starts, stops, kills, health changes. It shows a restart loop as it happens.

steps.title: Exercise: three reports
steps.text:
For each report, name the first command you would run and what you expect it to tell you.

1. "The worker container is in the list as `Exited (127)` and never did anything."
2. "The web service is up, but the page will not load from my browser."
3. "We redeployed the database and all the tasks are gone."

steps.title: One possible answer
steps.text:
1. `docker logs worker`, expecting a "not found" message. Code 127 means the start command is not in the image. Look for a typing error in `command:` or `CMD`, or a file that was never copied in.
2. `docker ps`, to read the ports column. No arrow means the port was never published. With an arrow, check the number after it, then the address the program listens on.
3. `docker inspect` on the database container, to list its mounts. Expect to find either no volume or one mounted at the wrong folder, which means the data lived in the old container's writable layer. Then check `docker volume ls` in case an older volume still holds it.

questions.prompt: What happened, and what do you do?

choices.text: The stop request was not handled, so use the exec form
choices.feedback: That also gives 137, but only after someone stops the container. Nobody did, and `OOMKilled` is true.

choices.text: It went over its memory limit. Find out why memory grows, then set a limit that fits
choices.feedback: The kernel killed it for exceeding the limit. Watch `docker stats`: steady growth is a leak to fix in the program, and a level that is merely above the limit means the limit is too low.

choices.text: The image is damaged, so pull it again
choices.feedback: A damaged image would fail at the start, not after an hour of running.

questions.prompt: What is wrong?

choices.text: The port is not published
choices.feedback: `3000/tcp` with no arrow only records what the image exposes. The container needs `-p 3000:3000`. `EXPOSE` by itself opens nothing.

choices.text: The program listens on `127.0.0.1`
choices.feedback: That is the next thing to check once a port is published. Here nothing is published at all.

choices.text: The container is on the wrong network
choices.feedback: Networks matter between containers. From the host, the published port is what counts.

lessons.title: Review and containerize an app
lessons.intro: This last module has no new ideas. It asks you to use the earlier ones together, twice: first to review a setup that works and has many faults, then to plan how to containerize a small application from a description. Do each exercise on paper before reading the answer. The reviewing is the useful part.

steps.title: How to review
steps.text:
A setup that runs can still be slow to build, unsafe, fragile or impossible to roll back. Reading for those faults is a skill of its own, and it gets quicker with a fixed list of questions.

| Question | Module |
| --- | --- |
| Is every image named by a specific version? | Images |
| What does the build context contain, and what is copied? | Dockerfile |
| Does a source change rebuild the dependencies? | Layers |
| Is the start command in exec form? | Start |
| Are settings and secrets outside the image? | Config |
| Where does each piece of data live? | Storage |
| Which ports are published, and to whom? | Network |
| Does anything wait for readiness, restart, or have a limit? | Health |
| Does the image hold only what runs? | Small |
| Which user does it run as? | Privilege |
| Can each release be identified and brought back? | Ship |

steps.title: Review 1: a Dockerfile
steps.text:
This Dockerfile builds and the service works. Find as many problems as you can. There are at least eight. For each, say what could go wrong.

Then continue.

steps.title: The most urgent one
steps.text: You have read the Dockerfile above. The image is pushed to a registry that every employee, and several outside contractors, can pull from.

steps.title: Review 1: what is wrong
steps.text:
1. **`FROM node:latest`.** The base can change to a new major version on any rebuild. Name a version.
2. **`COPY . .` before the install.** Any source change reinstalls every dependency. Copy the dependency list first.
3. **`COPY . .` with a `.env` in the project.** Unless a `.dockerignore` excludes it, the file is in the image.
4. **`ENV DATABASE_PASSWORD=...`.** A secret stored in the image, readable by anyone who can pull it.
5. **`apt-get` in two steps, with no cleanup.** The install can run against stale lists, and the lists stay in a layer.
6. **`vim` and `net-tools`.** Tools that the service does not use, shipped to production.
7. **`npm install`.** It may pick newer versions than the ones tested, and it includes development dependencies. `npm ci --omit=dev` installs exactly what the lock file names.
8. **No `USER`.** The service runs as root.
9. **Shell form `CMD`.** A shell is PID 1, so a stop waits ten seconds and then kills the service.
10. **A single stage on the full base.** The image is far larger than it needs to be.

A repaired version is below. It uses two stages only to keep build tools out, and it would work as one stage on the slim base for a project with no build step.

steps.title: Review 2: a Compose file
steps.text:
The same team's Compose file for production. Find the problems. There are at least seven.

Then continue.

steps.title: What a redeploy does
steps.text: You have read the Compose file above. The team upgrades the database by changing nothing and running `docker compose pull` and then `docker compose up -d`.

steps.title: Review 2: what is wrong
steps.text:
1. **`image: postgres` and `tracker:latest`.** Neither names a version. A pull can change the database's major version, and no release can be identified or rolled back.
2. **No volume on `db`.** The data is in the writable layer and is lost whenever the container is replaced.
3. **`5432:5432`.** The database is published to every machine that can reach the server. `web` reaches it over the network and needs no published port.
4. **The password in the file.** It is in version control. Use a secret file.
5. **`DATABASE_HOST: localhost`.** Inside `web`, that is `web` itself. It must be `db`.
6. **Short-form `depends_on` and no health check.** `web` can start before the database is ready.
7. **No restart policy.** Nothing comes back after a crash or a reboot.
8. **`privileged: true` and the Docker socket.** Either one hands the host to whoever takes over the service.
9. **No limits.** A leak in one service can take down the machine.

A repaired version is below.

steps.title: Design: containerize a notes application
steps.text:
A small team has a notes application that runs on one developer's laptop and nowhere else. Plan how to containerize it. You do not need to write every file. Decide, and give reasons.

- A **web service** that serves pages and an API on port 3000. It has a build step.
- A **worker** from the same code that creates search indexes in the background.
- A **PostgreSQL** database.
- **Attachments** that users upload, stored as files.
- It needs a database password and a key for an email provider.
- It will run on one server, and developers want to run all of it on their laptops.

Decide: how many images and how they are built, how each is tagged, what is published, where each kind of data lives, how settings and secrets arrive, what starts in which order, and how a release and a rollback happen.

steps.title: Design: one possible answer
steps.text:
**Images.** One image for the application, built in two stages: a build stage on the full base, and a final stage on the slim base running as an ordinary user, started in exec form. `web` and `worker` are two services from that one image with different commands. The database uses the official image, pinned to a version.

**Tags.** Each build is pushed as a version and as its commit identifier. The production file names the version.

**Network.** Only `web` is published, on the server's port 80. `db` is published nowhere. On laptops, an override file publishes the database on `127.0.0.1` for local tools.

**Data.** One volume for the database's files and one for attachments, mounted into both `web` and `worker`. Both are backed up, the database with its own dump tool. Logs go to output.

**Settings.** Ordinary values come from the environment through an `env_file`. The two secrets are files under `/run/secrets`, never in the image or in version control.

**Start.** `db` has a health check. A one-off `migrate` job waits for it. `web` and `worker` wait for the job to finish. All long-running services use `unless-stopped`, retry their connections, and have memory limits.

**Release.** Build once, test that image, then change the version in the production file and run `docker compose up -d`. A rollback is the previous version and the same command.

steps.title: Where to go next
steps.text:
This course stopped at one machine, deliberately. Everything in it still holds when you move to many machines, where a tool called an orchestrator starts containers across a group of servers, replaces failed ones and spreads traffic between them. Kubernetes is the best known. Images, tags, start commands, settings from outside, volumes, health checks and limits all appear there under similar names.

The habits are what carry over:

- An image holds what is the same everywhere. Settings and secrets come from outside.
- A container is disposable. Data lives in a volume.
- Name exact versions, build once, and promote the same image.
- Give a program the least power it can work with.
- When something fails, ask in order: state, output, exit code, what it sees.

questions.prompt: Which problem should be fixed first?

choices.text: The image is too large
choices.feedback: Size costs time and adds risk, but nothing is exposed by it today.

choices.text: The database password is stored in the image
choices.feedback: Everyone who can pull the image can read it with `docker inspect`. Remove it from the image, and then change the password, because the old one is in every copy that was ever pushed.

choices.text: The base image is `latest`
choices.feedback: That makes future builds unpredictable. It leaks nothing by itself.

questions.prompt: What happens to the notes in the database?

choices.text: They are lost if the database container is replaced
choices.feedback: The `db` service has no volume. If the pull brings a newer image, Compose replaces the container, and the data in the old writable layer goes with it.

choices.text: They are kept, because `up` reuses containers
choices.feedback: It reuses a container only when nothing about it changed. A newer image under the same tag is a change.

choices.text: They are kept in the image
choices.feedback: A container never writes to its image.

    image: registry.example.com/team/tracker:1.5.0

    user: node

    tmpfs: [/tmp]
    cap_drop: [ALL]
    mem_limit: 512m
    ports:
      - "80:3000"
    environment:
      DATABASE_HOST: db
      DATABASE_PASSWORD_FILE: /run/secrets/db_password
    secrets: [db_password]
    depends_on:
      db:
        condition: service_healthy

    image: postgres:17.2
    restart: unless-stopped
    mem_limit: 1g
    environment:
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD_FILE: /run/secrets/db_password
    secrets: [db_password]
    volumes:
      - db-data:/var/lib/postgresql/data
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD-SHELL", "pg_isready -U postgres"]
      interval: 5s
      retries: 5

    file: ./secrets/db_password.txt

  db-data:
